item.text: I’ll read the three parts in order, place each new note against the existing questions, write the JSONL update, then run the map check.

item.aggregated_output:
<<6:31 update 1, part 0 of 0..2>>
## THE CURRENT MAP
6:31/q01 Who are the people declared losers? [ٱلَّذِينَ كَذَّبُوا۟ · referent]
  6:31/q01/p1 Deniers of resurrection and the afterlife, especially the previously mentioned worldly life claimants; Quraysh and their followers are included. — reasons: Al-Tabari specifies resurrection, judgment, Paradise and Hell. Ibn ʿĀshūr points to 6:29 and 6:27 and says explicit naming develops their fate; Al-Ālūsī says the relative clause shows persistent denial caused their loss. Muqātil and Study Quran identify Quraysh/worldly life deniers.
6:31/q02 What reports identify a particular denier or occasion for this verse? [ٱلَّذِينَ كَذَّبُوا۟ · reports] (turns on: The reports name different people or give different statements.)
  6:31/q02/p1 Abū Jahl acknowledged Muhammad's truth but refused to follow a man from Banū ʿAbd Manāf. — reasons: Abū Yazīd al-Madanī reports a handshake and this statement before the verse was revealed.
  6:31/q02/p2 Abū Jahl said he did not call Muhammad a liar but rejected the message. — reasons: Nājiya ibn Kaʿb reports the verse followed this admission.
  6:31/q02/p3 Al-Ḥārith ibn ʿĀmir privately believed Muhammad truthful but feared Arab retaliation and loss of safety if he followed him. — reasons: Maqātil identifies him.
6:31/q03 What loss have the deniers incurred, and why? [خَسِرَ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the verse is explained as the failed faith transaction, squandered human capacities, or the word's basic lexical sense.)
  6:31/q03/p1 They forfeit afterlife reward and gain punishment by exchanging faith for unbelief. — reasons: Al-Ṭabarī likens faith and Paradise to the capital of a ruined transaction; Wāḥidī's authorities say the worst loss is one's soul, like losing a merchant's capital; Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies afterlife rather than worldly deprivation. Al-Rāzī counts lost reward and incurred punishment as two losses. Biqāʿī says every attainable reward is lost; Bayḍāwī adds lost blessing and enduring punishment; Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls it a failed bargain.
  6:31/q03/p2 They squander faculties meant for lasting knowledge and virtue on passing pleasure, and lack provisions for the afterlife. — reasons: Al-Rāzī names bodily and intellectual faculties as capital, transient pleasure as imagined profit, and alienation after death from both spiritual preparation and worldly attachments; Biqāʿī adds outer senses, reason and prophetic miracles. Study Quran relays Rāzī's investment analogy.
  6:31/q03/p3 Loss fundamentally means decrease, though some derive it from destruction. — reasons: Al-Jishumī reports both derivations.
6:31/q04 What does 'meeting God' mean here? [بِلِقَآءِ ٱللَّهِ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether meeting is understood as resurrection and recompense, an implied object such as reward, literal vision, or a representational encounter.)
  6:31/q04/p1 Resurrection, return to God, and His judgment and recompense. — reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās includes reward and punishment and cites 2:46; Ibn ʿAṭiyya includes God's power and the consequences of deeds; Rāzī says benefit and harm then lie with God alone. Kashshāf likens standing before the Lord to a guilty servant detained and rebuked. Qaffāl cites the warning concerning a false oath for property. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī observes the passage's progression from resurrection and gathering to meeting.
  6:31/q04/p2 Meeting God's promised reward and punishment, or the recompense of one's deeds, is figuratively called meeting God. — reasons: Wāḥidī cites ordinary speech about a dead person meeting his deeds; Ṭabrisī attributes the promise gloss to Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan; al-Ālūsī notes an implicit complement and possessive magnification in Abū Ḥayyān.
  6:31/q04/p3 The phrase retains actual meeting or vision of God. — reasons: Al-Qushayrī rejects extending contextual figurative uses to this verse and argues denial of God and His vision implies denial of existence; Nasafī notes denying resurrection also denies vision. Kashshāf reports full recognition of Him as another alternative.
  6:31/q04/p4 It pictures the afterlife's unimpeded manifestation of God's approval and wrath, like servants meeting their lord after absence. — reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts God's delayed worldly warning and choice with immediate afterlife consequences (18:49), and cites the hadith on loving to meet God and 40:15.
  6:31/q04/p5 Meeting primarily means encounter, with extended uses for sight, contemporaneity, calamity and battle. — reasons: Al-Jishumī gives the lexical range.
6:31/q05 What does 'until' terminate or connect? [حَتَّىٰٓ · grammar] (turns on: The syntactic reach of ḥattā and whether loss can end.)
  6:31/q05/p1 Their denial continues until the Hour, while their loss has no endpoint. — reasons: Wāḥidī, Zamakhsharī, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī and others say the governing verb is 'denied'; Ṭabrisī adds that regret then comes too late. Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects ending loss because its deprivation occurs at resurrection and not all deniers lose worldly goods.
  6:31/q05/p2 The ordinary loss lasts until Judgment, when a worse calamity eclipses it. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī analogizes Satan's curse 'until Judgment' at 38:78. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports and rejects commentators who end the loss there.
  6:31/q05/p3 Before 'when', ḥattā is initial and indicates cause rather than an endpoint. — reasons: Ibn al-Ḥājib says the sense is effectively 'when the Hour comes'.
6:31/q06 What event is 'the Hour' here? [ٱلسَّاعَةُ · referent] (turns on: Whether the lament and burden occur at actual resurrection, its onset, or death.)
  6:31/q06/p1 The resurrection, gathering and universal judgment. — reasons: Al-Ṭabarī specifies raising the dead from graves; Abū Ḥayyān argues simultaneous bearing of burdens better fits actual resurrection and says those in barzakh experience its interval as a day. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it the conventional name for resurrection and gathering.
  6:31/q06/p2 The moment resurrection begins, marked by sudden onset. — reasons: Wāḥidī prefers this because it accords with baghtatan; Elmalılı reports the onset time is known only to God.
  6:31/q06/p3 Death or one's personal Hour, the beginning of afterlife states. — reasons: Zamakhsharī and Rāzī cite the saying that whoever dies has had his resurrection/Hour; Biqāʿī and Elmalılı call death the beginning of transition. Al-Ālūsī reports death as the referent. Abū Ḥayyān argues actual resurrection fits better.
  6:31/q06/p4 The Hour is so close after death that it strikes like an immediate surprise. — reasons: Kashshāf offers this alternative.
6:31/q07 Why is it called 'the Hour'? [ٱلسَّاعَةُ · rhetoric] (turns on: The proposed relation of the name to speed, sudden onset, brevity, or fame.)
  6:31/q07/p1 Reckoning and recompense occur swiftly. — reasons: Wāḥidī, Qurṭubī, Samīn and Elmalılı explain the name through rapid accounting; al-Ālūsī says sāʿa first denotes a short interval.
  6:31/q07/p2 It arrives at an unexpected, unknown instant. — reasons: Wāḥidī prefers sudden onset because baghtatan follows; Elmalılı says only God knows its hour.
  6:31/q07/p3 Its duration is brief compared with eternity. — reasons: Nasafī compares the intervening interval with the eternal sequel; al-Ālūsī also reports this.
  6:31/q07/p4 The definite article identifies the known, uniquely famous Hour. — reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says it is established in minds and implied by meeting God; Samīn compares 'the star' and al-Thurayyā. Al-Ṭabarī calls it the known Hour.
6:31/q08 What does 'suddenly' convey? [بَغْتَةًۭ · meaning]
  6:31/q08/p1 An unforeseen onset without knowing its time or receiving warning. — reasons: Al-Zajjāj cites Arab usage and a poem of unforeseen death; Ibn ʿAbbās says God alone knows the Hour; Samīn stresses mere speed of an expected event is insufficient and cites poetry. Biqāʿī says its precise time is unknowable even generally.
6:31/q09 How is 'baghtatan' parsed? [بَغْتَةًۭ · grammar] (turns on: Whether the accusative describes a state or supplies/emphasizes a verbal action.)
  6:31/q09/p1 An accusative circumstantial verbal noun describing the Hour or those it overtakes. — reasons: Naḥḥās and Ibn ʿAṭiyya cite Sībawayh's nonproductive parallel qataltuhu ṣabran; Naḥḥās adds a poetic laʾyan bi-laʾy. Abū Ḥayyān allows either subject or object as its possessor.
  6:31/q09/p2 An absolute or cognate accusative, possibly supplied by an implied verb. — reasons: Kashshāf and Nasafī allow a verbal noun of surprise; Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn distinguish an omitted verb from the root or an omitted 'they came'; al-Ālūsī accepts these alternatives.
6:31/q10 What reports describe the Hour's arrival? [جَآءَتْهُمُ ٱلسَّاعَةُ بَغْتَةًۭ · reports] (turns on: The reports describe different preceding circumstances.)
  6:31/q10/p1 It can arrive while someone eats or two people trade, leaving their acts unfinished. — reasons: Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmits the Prophetic report through Abū Hurayra.
  6:31/q10/p2 A caller will announce the Hour three times before it arrives. — reasons: Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports ʿIkrima.
6:31/q11 How does 'jāʾa' here relate to Qur'anic use of 'atā'? [جَآءَتْهُمُ · links]
  6:31/q11/p1 Its force depends on the full verse and context; the supplied comparison is not completed. — reasons: Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts the Hour here and 6:40–41; his other discussion describes Ghāfir 40:82–85, where peoples mocked messengers and believed only after seeing punishment, too late to help. He cautions against isolating either verb.
6:31/q12 What does 'ḥasra' mean? [حَسْرَتَنَا · meaning]
  6:31/q12/p1 Intense regret or grief for something lost. — reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses it as regret. Baghawī compares a traveler whose mount fails; al-Rāghib derives it from exposure or exhausted strength. Ṭabrisī says remorse exhausts the regretful.
6:31/q13 What does calling out to 'our regret' do? [يَٰحَسْرَتَنَا · rhetoric] (turns on: Whether the figurative address is described as summoning regret or alerting the hearers.)
  6:31/q13/p1 It figuratively summons regret
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

<<6:31 update 1, part 1 of 0..2>>
 as if its appointed moment has arrived, magnifying anguish. — reasons: Sībawayh explains 'O wonder/regret, come'; Zajjāj, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurṭubī, Samīn and others say the abstraction cannot literally answer. Samīn adds rebuke for causing this need; Biqāʿī says the image warns others. Ibn ʿĀshūr says 'our' fixes their own fate, unlike a bare cry often made for others; the following ʿalā marks the cause.
  6:31/q13/p2 It alerts listeners to the terrible loss; the apparent addressee is the audience, not regret. — reasons: Zajjāj cites 'do not let me see you here' as an analogous displaced addressee; Sībawayh uses 'O wonder'; Wāḥidī cites 36:30, 39:56, 11:72 and 12:84. Ibn al-Jawzī cites 'O horses of God, ride'.
6:31/q14 What are they lamenting? [عَلَىٰ مَا فَرَّطْنَا فِيهَا · interpretation] (turns on: Whether their regret is specified as missed deeds, lost Paradise homes, mocked messengers, the failed bargain, or wasted faculties.)
  6:31/q14/p1 Neglected faith, obedience and preparation for Paradise and the Hereafter. — reasons: Al-Suddī specifies deeds that would earn Paradise; Muqātil names remembrance of God; Rāzī says lost reward, while their burdens indicate earned punishment. Biqāʿī includes disciplining the soul and following messengers; Wāḥidī, Baghawī and Study Quran specify afterlife work during worldly life.
  6:31/q14/p2 They see the Paradise places they have lost and lament. — reasons: A Prophetic report is transmitted by al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Qurṭubī, Ṭabrisī, Durr and Ṭabāṭabāʾī; Durr calls its chain sound. Samīn rejects the proposed pronoun reference to those places as remote; al-Ālūsī says the report cannot settle that reference.
  6:31/q14/p3 They regret having mocked the messengers. — reasons: Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmits Mujāhid.
  6:31/q14/p4 They regret the ruined transaction of trading faith and Paradise for disbelief and punishment. — reasons: Al-Ṭabarī infers the bargain from khusira; Qurṭubī cites 2:16.
  6:31/q14/p5 They lament wasted capacities and separation from former pleasures. — reasons: Al-Rāzī says God-given faculties were meant to disclose enduring truth and virtue; after death they are unprepared for the spiritual realm and cut off from transient pleasures. Study Quran relays him.
6:31/q15 What does 'farraṭnā' mean and derive from? [فَرَّطْنَا · meaning] (turns on: Whether tafrīṭ is explained by ordinary neglect or by its figurative derivation from precedence.)
  6:31/q15/p1 We neglected, wasted, or fell short of what we could have done. — reasons: Zajjāj includes incapacity or neglect; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān stress that action remained possible; Ṭabrisī contrasts tafrīṭ as falling behind with ifrāṭ as excess. Abū ʿUbayda and others give waste/neglect.
  6:31/q15/p2 It evokes going ahead or letting another precede one, with the doubled form removing precedence. — reasons: Zajjāj and Wāḥidī describe putting shortcoming first; Ibn Baḥr explains yielding one's lead. Samīn likens the privative formation to skinning a camel and compares 17:79; al-Ālūsī repeats this morphological account. Qurṭubī says they let others precede them in obedience.
6:31/q16 What is the grammatical role of 'mā' in their lament? [مَا فَرَّطْنَا · grammar] (turns on: Whether mā names the act of neglect or the things neglected.)
  6:31/q16/p1 It is a verbal noun: they lament their neglect. — reasons: Samīn says 'for what we neglected' attaches to regret.
  6:31/q16/p2 It is a relative pronoun for deeds or acts of obedience they neglected. — reasons: Ṭabrisī and al-Ālūsī say on this analysis the antecedent is explicit in their speech; Abū Ḥayyān and Rāzī also report it.
6:31/q17 What does the pronoun in 'fīhā' refer to? [فِيهَا · referent] (turns on: Which implied antecedent—world, Hour, Paradise, bargain, deeds, or Paradise places—fits the context.)
  6:31/q17/p1 Worldly life, where they neglected work for the afterlife. — reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil say the unmentioned world is obvious from context; Rāzī says reason identifies it as the place of neglect.
  6:31/q17/p2 The Hour and the faith and preparation it required. — reasons: Al-Ḥasan and others construe 'in it' as neglecting its affairs or preparation; Kashshāf compares 'I neglected God's side' at 39:56.
  6:31/q17/p3 Paradise, which they failed to seek and work for. — reasons: Al-Suddī gives this reading and Ṭabrisī pairs it with the report of Hell's people seeing their Paradise homes. Al-Ālūsī considers it remote.
  6:31/q17/p4 The transaction implied by their loss. — reasons: Al-Ṭabarī argues loss implies sale, even without an explicit noun; Ibn ʿAṭiyya notes the implied bargain. Al-Ālūsī considers the reading remote. Samīn attributes it to al-Ḥasan.
  6:31/q17/p5 The good deeds or acts of obedience expressed by a relative 'mā'. — reasons: Wāḥidī, Rāzī and al-Ālūsī note this makes the pronoun refer to an item in the utterance itself; Ibn al-Jawzī reports obedience as the antecedent.
  6:31/q17/p6 Their former places in Paradise. — reasons: Samīn reports and rejects this proposal as remote.
6:31/q18 How does 'while they carry' attach to the lament? [وَهُمْ يَحْمِلُونَ · grammar] (turns on: Whether the state is simultaneous with the cry or anticipated.)
  6:31/q18/p1 It is a circumstantial clause describing them as they speak. — reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Samīn, Bursevī and al-Ālūsī identify the wāw as circumstantial; Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn say the explicit subject pronoun strengthens attribution.
  6:31/q18/p2 The burden-bearing may be prospective relative to the lament. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī permits this alternate timing.
6:31/q19 What are 'their awzār'? [أَوْزَارَهُمْ · meaning] (turns on: Whether awzār names sins, their punishment, divine wrath, ignored reminders, or inward attachments.)
  6:31/q19/p1 Their sins, errors and evil deeds, described as heavy burdens. — reasons: Ibn Qutayba cites 94:2–3; Ibn ʿAbbās and many others gloss sin; Qatāda says the load is their deeds and also their work or earning. Ṭabarī rejects physical-load gloss as unattested Arab usage, preferring the sinning sense. Asad adopts Ibn ʿAbbās through Rāzī.
  6:31/q19/p2 The punishment or suffering earned by their sins. — reasons: Naḥḥās records this as a second gloss; Zajjāj and others compare severe punishment to a crushing load, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī includes sin's consequence among possibilities.
  6:31/q19/p3 God's wrath earned by sin. — reasons: Study Quran cites 2:61, 2:90, 3:112 and 3:162.
  6:31/q19/p4 The reminders and warnings they ignored. — reasons: Study Quran cites 20:100–101, where the reminder becomes an afterlife burden.
  6:31/q19/p5 For the veiled soul, attachments, bodily love, sins and sensory traits rooted within it. — reasons: Qāshānī says these bind, veil and torment the person.
6:31/q20 What is the root sense and derivation of 'wizr'? [أَوْزَارَهُمْ · meaning] (turns on: Whether the lexical starting point is carried weight or a refuge/support.)
  6:31/q20/p1 A heavy load; sins are named for the weight one carries. — reasons: Ibn Qutayba cites 94:2–3; Abū ʿUbayd describes carrying goods in a cloak and the loads of war. Wāḥidī cites 6:164; Samīn gives awzār as plural of wizr, war equipment and a poetic line, and wazīr as bearer of a ruler's burdens. Akhfash gives wazara/yaziru/wizran and mawzūr; Yūnus notes two vocalizations. Funeral usage prefers mawzūrāt over common maʾzūrāt, while Abū ʿAlī calls the latter sound-following.
  6:31/q20/p2 A mountain refuge or support on which one relies; heaviness and support extend to sin and a minister. — reasons: Zajjāj and Abū ʿUbayd cite Moses' request for Aaron as minister (20:29–30); Samīn and al-Rāghib cite 75:11. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls derivation from a refuge or helper unclear.
6:31/q21 How are their burdens borne 'on their backs'? [يَحْمِلُونَ أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the image presents embodied deeds, metaphorical hardship, constant attachment, or an inward state.)
  6:31/q21/p1 Literally: deeds take visible forms, and the sinner's ugly, foul deed rides or is carried on his back. — reasons: Muqātil says the deed demands to be carried; reports from al-Suddī, ʿAmr, Abū Marzūq and ʿUmayr include a grave-companion, a public exposure or a journey to Hell. Some describe the believer's fragrant good deed as a mount (19:85). Bursevī argues afterlife deeds can become visible though accidents here; al-Ālūsī sees no obstacle and cites Sunni belief in embodied deeds and weighing. Abū Ḥayyān's preferred report groups ʿUmayr, ʿAmr, al-Suddī and Ṭabarī.
  6:31/q21/p2 Figuratively: sins and their painful punishment weigh on them like loads. — reasons: Zajjāj says Arabic uses 'heavy' for severe aversion; Ibn ʿAṭiyya treats back-bearing as an intensified figure and questions the refuge derivation. Zamakhsharī compares hands as the normal instrument of deeds in 42:30; Bursevī calls sins bodily loads by metaphor.
  6:31/q21/p3 The image says sins never leave or release them. — reasons: Arabists compare a person always before one's eyes to one continually in mind; Nasafī and Qurṭubī say sin clings to the denier.
  6:31/q21/p4 Inwardly, rooted traits and attachments veil and torment the soul. — reasons: Qāshānī calls this the burden of bodily love and sensory traits.
6:31/q22 Why mention the backs specifically? [عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ · rhetoric]
  6:31/q22/p1 The back is the customary and strongest place for heavy burdens, intensifying their weight. — reasons: Ṭabarī notes loads might otherwise be borne on head or shoulder; Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn say the back carries more, with Samīn comparing the hand's touch in 6:7. Kashshāf contrasts hand imagery for earned deeds in 42:30.
6:31/q23 What does 'alā' add? [أَلَا · rhetoric]
  6:31/q23/p1 It announces and intensifies the gravity of the condemnation. — reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya compares Prophetic calls to convey and witness; Nasafī and Biqāʿī emphasize severity.
6:31/q24 What is condemned by 'evil is what they bear'? [سَآءَ مَا يَزِرُونَ · interpretation] 
<<part 1 ends; continues in part 2>>

<<6:31 update 1, part 2 of 0..2>>
(turns on: Whether the closing blame points to the evil burden itself or its recompense.)
  6:31/q24/p1 Their vile burden of sins or evil deeds. — reasons: ʿAbd al-Razzāq and Qatāda gloss the act as what they do; Ibn ʿAbbās calls it a wretched load. Zamakhsharī compares 7:177; Rāzī points to 4:22; Biqāʿī says the rebuke gathers its many defects and unbearable weight.
  6:31/q24/p2 The punishment they suffer as recompense for evil deeds. — reasons: Ṭabrisī records this second sense.
6:31/q25 How can 'sāʾa mā yazirūn' be parsed? [سَآءَ مَا يَزِرُونَ · grammar] (turns on: Whether sāʾa functions as an ordinary verb, exclamation, or biʾsa-like blame.)
  6:31/q25/p1 A plain transitive past verb with mā as subject and an omitted object. — reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites a poem; Samīn says mā may be relative, verbal or indefinite and notes the Shaykh will not fix the poem to a single parse. Al-Ālūsī lists the same mā options.
  6:31/q25/p2 An exclamatory expression: how awful what they carry. — reasons: Samīn says this reading is fixed and intransitive, with ḍamma on the second radical; al-Ālūsī accepts it.
  6:31/q25/p3 An intensified verb of blame equivalent to biʾsa. — reasons: Zajjāj compares 7:177, Samīn refers to mā in 2:90; the Shaykh distinguishes its subject rules and clause structure, but Samīn says the distinction needs interpretation. Ibn ʿAṭiyya permits this beside a declarative reading.
6:31/q26 What do the burdens teach about the deniers' two losses? [يَٰحَسْرَتَنَا أَوْزَارَهُمْ · interpretation]
  6:31/q26/p1 They failed to gain the reward they could have prepared for, while earning punishment through sins. — reasons: Al-Rāzī pairs regret for omitted provision with burdens of committed wrong; Bursevī contrasts absent good deeds and physically borne sins; Elmalılı pairs loss of reward with enormous punishment.
6:31/q27 What inward reading is given to denial, the Hour, and burdens? [* · inward] (turns on: Whether the inward burden is embedded traits broadly or the self itself.)
  6:31/q27/p1 The veiled deny meeting the Real; minor resurrection exposes neglected work and attachments embedded in the soul. — reasons: Qāshānī says bodily love, sin and sensory habits become the burdens that obstruct aims and torment the self.
  6:31/q27/p2 The self and its very existence are the chief burden; repentance and effacement free the seeker by God's aid. — reasons: Bursevī cites Ḥāfiẓ against self-regard, a saying that the self cannot escape itself, and Tirmidhī on remembrance softening the heart while ego hardens it. Divine unity and following its people sustain spiritual life.
6:31/q28 What does the pilgrimage dream illustrate about release from burdens? [* · inward]
  6:31/q28/p1 Sound-hearted companionship with the holy benefits the seeker, as following and hearing the Prophet could have relieved deniers' burdens. — reasons: Bursevī tells ʿAlī ibn al-Muwaffaq's dream: after giving up his litter to walk among pilgrims, maidens washed his feet and counted him among them because he loved their company. God guides whom He wills.
6:31/q29 How does this verse connect with its surrounding passage? [* · links] (turns on: Whether the pictured encounter is tied to universal resurrection or each death.)
  6:31/q29/p1 It completes the portrait of people claiming worldly life alone, showing the afterlife loss their denial entails. — reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the opening a fresh calamity report; Ibn ʿĀshūr says explicit naming makes their fate an independent statement; Ṭabāṭabāʾī links resurrection, gathering, the Hereafter and meeting God. Study Quran cites 6:29 and locates 4–31 among responses to Makkan excuses and earlier destroyed peoples; Iṣlāḥī contrasts Quran rejecters with afterlife deniers.
  6:31/q29/p2 The scene may portray each unbeliever's encounter with the afterlife after death. — reasons: Kur'an Yolu prefers this explanation: souls already dead see their error now and future dead will do so; the alternative treats prophetic past tense for future resurrection as a mark of certainty.
6:31/q30 What general pattern of human loss does the verse illustrate? [* · theology]
  6:31/q30/p1 Wrong paths defeat the goals for which the created order provides proper causes; apparent unjust gain ends in loss. — reasons: Ṭabāṭabāʾī compares trying to sustain life without eating and digestion. Belief in God and the afterlife and practical law are routes to happiness; shirk, seizure of property, violation of honor or life, neglect of worship and deceit damage connected causes in this life and next.
6:31/q31 What encounter with God is reported for a denier? [بِلِقَآءِ ٱللَّهِ · reports]
  6:31/q31/p1 God reminds the denier of His gifts, and the servant admits having forgotten God. — reasons: Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmits the report through Abū Hurayra.
6:31/q32 What is the clause structure around 'when they said'? [إِذَا قَالُوا۟ · grammar]
  6:31/q32/p1 'They said' answers the conditional 'when'. — reasons: Samīn and Ibn ʿĀshūr make the cry the apodosis; al-Ālūsī says the conditional is answered by 'O our remorse'.
6:31/q33 How does the preceding challenge 'Is this not the truth?' relate to denial here? [* · links]
  6:31/q33/p1 The challenge rebukes denial of resurrection and recompense, and the ensuing punishment answers their disbelief. — reasons: Kashshāf explains the previous question and punishment; Kur'an Yolu says after death the denier recognizes the error. Ibn ʿĀshūr says deferred warning in this life yields immediate consequences in the next.
6:31/q34 What do other terms in the adjacent verse mean? [* · links]
